title: Building soil through the year
teaches: Year-round habits that protect soil structure, seasonal bed care from autumn through summer, and using cover crops and mulch to feed soil life.

blocks.text: When the autumn harvest finishes and the vegetable beds are full of spent stalks, older gardening books advise pulling everything up and digging the plot bare for winter. The biology and physics from the previous six lessons point toward leaving the ground intact and covered instead.

Good soil care comes down to a few steady practices.[^principles] Keeping the surface covered shields soil crumbs from baking sun and heavy rain (lessons 2 and 5). Keeping living roots in the ground for as many months as possible pumps sugars into the underground food web (lesson 3). Adding compost or organic mulch each year replaces the organic matter that microbes consume (lesson 4), while skipping unnecessary digging and staying off the beds preserves pore spaces and fungal networks (lesson 5). Practiced together, these habits improve a garden's tilth and fertility year after year.

blocks.caption: A mulched bed protected from rain, fed from the surface, and left undug

blocks.text: You can even start a brand-new bed over lawn or weeds without touching a spade. Mow the grass short, lay down overlapping sheets of plain corrugated cardboard with any plastic tape removed, soak the cardboard thoroughly, and spread 10 to 15 cm of finished compost on top. You can plant seedlings or seeds directly into the compost that same afternoon. Deprived of light, the turf dies and decays while earthworms pull the softening cardboard down into their burrows, leaving a friable, undug bed by the following year.[^no-dig]

blocks.title: Core ideas
points: Soil structure and fertility grow when beds stay covered, rooted, fed from the surface, and undisturbed.
Protecting existing soil crumbs and root channels matters just as much as adding fresh compost.

blocks.text: The interactive wheel below tracks a single garden bed across the four seasons, starting with a traditional routine: growing a summer vegetable crop, digging the soil over in autumn, and leaving it bare until spring. Adjust the seasonal covers and digging settings to see how the bed's [[organic matter|organic]] responds over a five-year span.[^model]

blocks.caption: Seasonal bed management and its effect on soil organic matter over five years
blocks.task: Raise the bed's organic matter by at least half a percent in five years

blocks.text: Raising a soil's total organic matter by half a percentage point takes several years because microbes respire most added carbon back into the air. Even so, the physical improvements show up much faster at the surface. A bed tucked under mulch or a cover crop for a single winter crumbles easily when you plant into it the next spring, and a plot left undug for two years develops surface worm casts and drains cleanly after downpours.[^broadbalk]

blocks.title: Seasonal bed routine
points: In late summer and autumn, cut finished crops off at the soil line with secateurs and leave the roots in place to decay. Sow a winter cover crop right away, or blanket the soil with fallen leaves, straw, or 5 cm of compost.
During winter, keep the soil surface covered and avoid stepping on the beds, especially when wet soil is easy to compact.

In spring, chop the cover crop down at ground level two to four weeks before planting and leave the clippings on the surface as mulch, or cover the bed with an opaque tarp for a few weeks to smother the growth before planting through the residue.[^terminating]
Throughout summer, space crops closely so their leaves shade the ground, tuck straw or compost mulch between rows to slow evaporation, and replant empty spots as soon as early harvests finish.

blocks.text: Gardeners sow a **cover crop** (sometimes called green manure) to protect and enrich the soil between food harvests rather than to fill the kitchen basket. Different plant families do different jobs underground: cereal grasses like winter rye and oats weave a dense fibrous root mat and produce abundant straw, brassicas like mustard and daikon (forage) radish grow rapidly in cool weather and drive thick taproots through compacted layers, and legumes like crimson clover, hairy vetch, field beans, and Austrian winter peas partner with root bacteria to capture nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into plant-available fertilizer.[^rhizobia]

blocks.caption: A dense cover crop shielding the soil surface and feeding microbes through its roots

blocks.text: Match the cover crop to the calendar. In early autumn, about four to six weeks before your first hard frost, sow winter-hardy species like cereal rye, hairy vetch, field beans, or a mixture of rye and winter peas; cereal rye germinates in cooler soil than any other cover crop if you are planting late. Alternatively, sowing spring oats or daikon radish in late summer gives you a thick autumn carpet that winter frost kills naturally, leaving a ready-made mulch by spring with no chopping required. For short four-to-six-week gaps between summer vegetables, fast-blooming buckwheat or phacelia covers bare soil quickly and feeds pollinators. The course reference page lists sowing rates and seasons, and if you cannot sow seed in time, a 5 cm layer of autumn leaves or compost will still protect the surface over winter.

blocks.title: Field checks for your garden
points: Sketch a four-season plan for one of your vegetable beds, noting what will cover the soil in spring, summer, autumn, and winter without digging.
This autumn, protect at least one finished bed with either a winter cover crop or a 5 cm blanket of chopped leaves or compost, and compare its tilth next spring against an uncovered spot.

blocks.caption: Questions on seasonal soil care and cover crops
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.question: Once autumn harvests finish, how should you prepare a vegetable bed for winter?
options: Cover the soil with a winter cover crop, organic mulch, or compost
Dig the soil over deeply and leave the clods bare to weather
Water the bare bed heavily every week
items.why: A living cover crop or mulch layer shields soil crumbs from winter rain impact and prevents nutrients from leaching away, whereas bare dug soil crusts and erodes.

items.question: Why do gardeners plant cover crops between vegetable harvests?
options: To shield the soil surface, feed microbes via living roots, and add organic matter
To harvest and sell the roots as a cash crop
To dry out waterlogged summer beds before autumn rain
items.why: Cover crops protect the surface from erosion, pump root exudates into the soil food web, scavenge leftover nutrients, and decompose into organic matter.

items.question: Which group of cover crops adds new nitrogen to the soil from the air?
options: Legumes such as clovers, vetch, peas, and field beans
Cereal grasses such as winter rye and oats
Brassicas such as mustards and forage radishes
items.why: Legumes house symbiotic rhizobia bacteria inside nodules on their roots that convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonium that plants can use.

items.question: How do you manage a living winter cover crop in spring before planting vegetables?
options: Cut it down at ground level a few weeks before planting and leave the residue on top as mulch
Rototill the green stems deeply into the bed and sow small seeds the same afternoon
Pull the entire plants up by the roots and burn them
items.why: Chopping the stems at the base (especially once the crop reaches flowering) and leaving them on the surface creates a protective mulch while the roots decay undisturbed underground. Waiting two to three weeks before planting avoids temporary nitrogen tie-up and seed-corn maggots.

items.question: How does a surface mulch of straw or fallen leaves affect a garden bed in summer?
options: It slows evaporation, cushions the impact of rain, buffers soil temperature, and feeds earthworms
It strips nitrogen out of the entire root zone down to 30 cm
It serves only a cosmetic purpose without changing soil moisture
items.why: Surface mulch shades the soil, cuts evaporative water loss, keeps roots cooler in summer heat, and decomposes gradually from the bottom up. Because high-carbon straw sits on top rather than being dug into the root zone, microbes immobilize nitrogen only at the thin soil-mulch boundary.

items.question: A gardener spreads compost on a bed every year but double-digs the soil each spring and autumn. How does all that digging affect the soil?
options: Digging shatters soil aggregates and flushes the bed with oxygen, causing microbes to burn through organic matter faster
Compost cannot decompose at all if it is buried by a spade
Frequent digging permanently doubles the soil's cation exchange capacity
items.why: Turning the soil breaks apart fungal hyphae and protective soil crumbs, exposing trapped organic carbon to oxygen and triggering a microbial feeding frenzy that releases that carbon as carbon dioxide.

items.question: How can you convert a patch of lawn into a vegetable bed without digging or tilling?
options: Lay plain cardboard over the mown grass, soak it, top with 10 to 15 cm of compost, and plant into the compost
Scrape off all the topsoil with a shovel and plant directly into the subsoil
Rototill the turf three times in wet weather
items.why: Overlapping cardboard blocks light so the sod dies in place and feeds earthworms, while the 10 to 15 cm layer of compost on top provides an immediate, weed-free root zone.

items.question: Why does a garden bed need fresh organic matter (from compost, mulch, or cover crops) nearly every year to maintain its level?
options: Soil microbes and invertebrates continually consume organic matter and respire most of its carbon as carbon dioxide
Organic matter chemically transforms into quartz sand over winter
A single summer rainstorm washes all humus out of the topsoil
items.why: Most fresh plant residue and compost is broken down by soil life within a year or two, releasing nutrients for crops while respiring carbon dioxide into the air.

learned: Healthy soil management rests on keeping the surface covered, maintaining living roots, adding organic matter, and avoiding unnecessary digging or compaction.
Cover finished beds immediately in autumn using cover crops, fallen leaves, straw, or compost, and establish new beds over grass using cardboard and compost rather than a spade.
Legume cover crops (clovers, vetch, peas, beans) fix atmospheric nitrogen, cereal grasses (rye, oats) build dense root mats and biomass, and brassicas (radishes, mustards) break up compacted layers.
Building total soil organic matter by a measurable percentage takes years, but undug, winter-covered beds show noticeably better crumb structure and drainage within a single season.
next: Lesson 9 pulls every test and observation together to diagnose problem beds and decide which fix to tackle first.

principles.title: Principles of soil health
principles.text: The US Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) summarizes soil health around four core principles: minimize soil disturbance, maximize soil cover, maximize continuous living roots, and maximize biodiversity (often adding livestock integration on farms). Agricultural researchers and home gardeners arrived at these practices independently through prairie no-till farming and British and American no-dig market gardening.

model.title: How the five-year simulation works
model.text: In the diagram's model, each seasonal cover adds a set amount of organic carbon per year, while soil microbes mineralize (burn through) a fraction of the bed's existing organic matter. Tilling and bare soil increase the mineralization rate and erosion loss. The rates are calibrated to match typical garden measurements (shifts of a few tenths of a percentage point per year), illustrating the direction and relative speed of management choices rather than predicting an exact lab test for your yard.

no-dig.title: Pioneers of no-dig gardening
no-dig.text: Starting in the 1940s in Connecticut, Ruth Stout popularized growing vegetables under a permanent 20 cm blanket of spoiled hay without ever tilling or spading. In England, market gardener Charles Dowding has run side-by-side strip trials of dug versus undug beds since 2007; his undug plots consistently yield as much or more produce than the dug strips while requiring less time weeding.

broadbalk.title: The Broadbalk wheat experiment
broadbalk.text: At Rothamsted Research in Hertfordshire, England, the Broadbalk field has grown winter wheat continuously since autumn 1843, comparing strips treated with farmyard manure, synthetic fertilizers, or nothing at all. Plots receiving annual farmyard manure now hold more than twice the soil organic carbon of the unmanured strips. Most of that carbon gain occurred during the first 50 years, demonstrating that depleted soil builds organic matter rapidly at first before leveling off at a new equilibrium where annual decay matches annual additions.

terminating.title: Killing a cover crop without digging
terminating.text: If you cut a winter-hardy cover crop like cereal rye or hairy vetch too early in spring while it is still lush and vegetative, it will simply regrow from the crown. Waiting until the crop begins to flower (or until rye stems reach the 'boot' stage and shed pollen) exhausts its root reserves so chopping or crimping kills it cleanly. If you need the bed earlier in spring, cut the crop at the base and cover the plot with a light-blocking silage tarp or sheet of cardboard for two to four weeks.

rhizobia.title: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation
rhizobia.text: Soil bacteria called **rhizobia** infect the root hairs of legumes (the pea and bean family, Fabaceae), prompting the plant to form small round root nodules. Inside these low-oxygen nodules, the bacteria use the enzyme nitrogenase to convert atmospheric nitrogen gas (N2) into ammonium (NH4+), trading that nitrogen to the plant in exchange for sugars made by photosynthesis. A vigorous winter crop of hairy vetch or crimson clover can fix 80 to 150 kg of nitrogen per hectare (8 to 15 grams per square metre) in a season. If you slice open an active nodule with a fingernail, the centre looks reddish-pink from leghemoglobin, an iron-containing protein closely related to human hemoglobin that regulates oxygen around the bacteria.
